meta.subtitle: Fiscal Q3 revenue rose 40% and adjusted operating margin reached 50.0%, but at 25.7x FY27E consensus EPS the upswing is largely in the price

analystCommentary:
ADI's fiscal third quarter 2026, ended August 1, 2026, was well ahead of a year earlier on revenue, margins and cash flow, and the company's outlook points to a higher fourth quarter. For a buyer at $420.83, the question is how much of the next year the price already carries.

In our reading, close to all of it. The valuation section shows the stock priced on fiscal 2027 consensus earnings, and the financials and risk sections show margins at a level the last downturn did not hold. Our scenarios therefore give a cyclical turn somewhat more weight than the upside case.

The franchise and the near-term momentum underpin our Base and Bull cases: the fourth-quarter outlook points up, and nothing in the current data shows the cycle turning. The moat section weighs how much of ADI's cash resilience in the last downturn came from pricing and how much from lower capital spending.

Weighted, the scenarios put fair value close to the current price, with a Bear case that would take the shares back to their 52-week low. That derives HOLD, and it sits nearer to SELL than to BUY.

executiveSummary.companyOverview:
Analog Devices, Inc. designs, manufactures, tests and markets integrated circuits, software and subsystems. Its products include data converters, power management and reference products, power ICs, amplifiers, radio frequency and microwave ICs, micro-electro-mechanical systems such as accelerometers, gyroscopes and inertial measurement units, isolators, and digital signal processing and system products. It serves industrial, automotive, consumer, instrumentation, aerospace, defense and healthcare, and communications customers through a direct sales force, third-party distributors, independent sales representatives and online. The company was incorporated in 1965 and is headquartered in Wilmington, Massachusetts.

ADI reports as a single segment. Fiscal 2025, which ended November 1, 2025, brought revenue of $11.0B, and the 10-Q under review covers the fiscal third quarter 2026, ended August 1, 2026. At $420.83 a share the market values the company at about $203.9B.

thesis.body:
HOLD, target range $400–$470. ADI is in a broad upswing: fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 40% year over year, adjusted operating margin reached 50.0%, and the company's fourth-quarter outlook points higher.

The price already leans on the next leg. At 25.7x FY27E consensus EPS of $16.35, the stock needs fiscal 2027 to bring a third straight year of growth. If growth stalls instead, as it did after FY22, the FY24 results show how far earnings can fall, and our Bear case prices that outcome with a lower multiple as well. Our weighted expected return of -0.8% derives HOLD.

catalysts: Fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results against the August 19, 2026 outlook of $4.3 billion in revenue, plus or minus $100 million.
The outlook for the opening quarter of fiscal 2027, the year the thesis turns on.
Further growth in the data center sub-market, which the company says led growth within Communications.
The pace of buybacks, which together with dividends ran above free cash flow over the trailing twelve months.
risks: A stall in fiscal 2027 growth that the market reads as the start of a downturn, from margins above every fiscal year in the table.
A de-rating from near the top of the 52-week range if FY27E estimates slip.
Export restrictions affecting China, which the fiscal 2025 10-K says have already affected revenue.
Reliance on distributors, which carried 58% of third-quarter revenue.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Fiscal third-quarter 2026 revenue was $4.02 billion, {+ up 40% +} year over year, and nine-month revenue rose 36%. The company attributes the increase to "broad-based demand across end markets"; the growth section covers the end-market detail.

Gross margin rose to 67.3% from 62.1%, a gain of 520 basis points that ADI attributes "primarily" to "higher utilization of our manufacturing fixed costs as a result of increased customer demand and favorable mix of products sold into our end markets." Operating margin reached 40.1% against 28.4% a year earlier. R&D expenses rose 17% and SMG&A expenses 22%, yet they fell to 13% and 10% of revenue from 16% and 11%, which the company credits to "higher revenue levels and improved operating leverage."

Reported EPS growth overstates the operating gain. Diluted EPS rose 163% to $2.74 from $1.04, but the year-ago effective tax rate of 32.1%, against 13.3% this quarter, was higher "primarily due to" a $153.8 million net deferred tax expense tied to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. This quarter's special charges line also includes a $24.4 million gain on the sale of a subsidiary in Penang, Malaysia. Operating income, which sits above the tax line, rose 97% to $1,613 million from $818 million, and that is the cleaner measure of the year's gain.

Adjusted diluted EPS rose 68% to $3.45 from $2.05, and adjusted operating margin reached 50.0% from 42.2%. The release defines adjusted EPS as excluding acquisition-related expenses, acquisition-related transaction costs, special charges, net, and tax related items, which it defines as the income tax effect of those exclusions; on that definition, it does not clearly remove the year-ago tax charge. Its use here is that the consensus EPS figures appear to sit on the same basis, as the valuation section explains.

Profitability is now above anything in the five-year table. The trailing operating margin of 35.5% compares with no more than 31.1% (FY23) in any fiscal year shown. That reads as a cyclically high level rather than a new floor; the risk section sets out what the last downturn did to margins.
financials.balanceCommentary:
Liquidity has tightened since fiscal year-end. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments were $2.3 billion at August 1, 2026, well below the $3.7B of cash and short-term investments at fiscal 2025 year-end (November 1, 2025), and the trailing current ratio of 1.25 compares with 2.19 at that year-end. The capital allocation section sets the cash decline against shareholder returns. The 10-Q gives no updated debt figure, so fiscal 2025's total debt of $8.6B is the latest shown, and we do not restate net debt for the quarter.

Approximately $1.0 billion of the August cash was held in the United States and the balance in foreign subsidiaries, so more than half sits offshore. ADI says it does not expect current regulatory restrictions or taxes on repatriation to have a material adverse effect on its liquidity, a view we accept, since the U.S. balance alone exceeds the third quarter's dividend payment.

Leverage is modest against current earnings, with trailing net debt/EBITDA of 1.0x and interest coverage of 14.1x. Those ratios rest on upswing EBITDA, though. Against FY24 EBITDA of $4.1B, the fiscal 2025 debt load would look noticeably heavier, which is the relevant test if the cycle turns.

ADI says it believes its liquidity, cash from operations and "existing and anticipated available short- and long-term financing" will be sufficient "for at least the next twelve months." The balance sheet is no constraint today, but it carries less cushion than at year-end.
financials.cashflowCommentary:
Cash generation is a clear strength. The release reports trailing-twelve-month operating cash flow of $5.5 billion and free cash flow of $4.9 billion. That free cash flow is a higher share of revenue than the 29.8% trailing net margin, so cash earnings run ahead of reported earnings.

Conversion slipped over the nine months. Operating cash flow was 36% of revenue against 39% a year earlier, even as net income rose 126%. ADI attributes the higher operating cash flow to "higher net income adjusted for non-cash items", which leaves the lower ratio unexplained; it is a ratio to track rather than a warning.

Capital spending is light: FY25 capital expenditure was $533.6M, so nearly all operating cash reaches free cash flow. The moat section looks at how the timing of capital spending has moved the free-cash-flow margin, and capital allocation covers whether shareholder returns now outrun the cash.

valuation.multiplesCommentary:
The shares trade at $420.83, near the top of a 52-week range of $223.47–$445.91, a sharp move off the low within a year. They have also risen sharply since early September, in the weeks after the August 19 results. None of the filings or releases we draw on explains either move, and we assign neither a cause, but both mean the starting multiple already reflects a strong run.

The headline multiples sit on different earnings bases. The trailing P/E of 49.9x rests on reported diluted EPS. The vendor labels 32.6x a forward (NTM) P/E, but it lines up with the current price over FY26E consensus EPS of $12.89, so it is in effect a multiple on the fiscal year now closing. The ~25.7x is on FY27E consensus EPS of $16.35. Both consensus EPS figures appear to be on the company's adjusted basis: nine-month reported diluted EPS of $6.83 plus the fourth-quarter reported EPS outlook of $3.14 falls well short of the FY26E figure. The step down from the trailing multiple to the FY27E multiple therefore mixes a change of earnings basis with expected growth, and only part of it is growth.

Trailing EV/EBITDA is 30.5x and the trailing free-cash-flow yield is 2.4%, against a dividend yield of 1.05%. No peer multiples are available, so we judge these against ADI's own earnings path. On that path, a cash yield that low leaves little cushion if fiscal 2027 falls short.

The Street is firmly positive: 30 of 34 analysts rate the stock Buy, 4 Hold and none Sell. The consensus target of $470.72 implies +11.9%, the median is $463.50, and targets run from $365.00 to $675.00, so the high end lifts the mean. Even the Street's central case leaves only moderate upside from here.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Basis: 32.6x, today's multiple on current-year (FY26E) consensus EPS, applied to FY27E consensus EPS of $16.35. Fiscal 2027 delivers consensus and, a year from now, the market still pays that current-year multiple. That needs demand to keep strengthening and investors to expect growth to continue into fiscal 2028, with adjusted margins near the fourth-quarter outlook.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Basis: the median Street target of $463.50, which values FY27E consensus EPS at a multiple between today's FY27E multiple and the current-year multiple in the Bull case. Fiscal 2027 delivers consensus, growth slows from the fiscal 2026 pace as consensus already expects, and the cycle does not turn within the year.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Basis: the 52-week low of $223.47, which values FY25 adjusted diluted EPS of $7.79 at a multiple between today's 25.7x FY27E multiple and the Bull's current-year multiple. Fiscal 2027 growth stalls, as FY23's did after FY22, and the market prices a decline like FY24's: earnings expectations fall back toward the fiscal 2025 level, and the shares give back the year's move.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
All three scenarios value ADI at a one-year horizon on earnings, targets or prices a reader can check above. They differ on whether fiscal 2027 brings the growth consensus expects, and on what the market pays for the result.

The Base case carries 55%, and it rests on fiscal 2027, for which no document we draw on gives a company figure, so the weight is a judgment. In its favor, the CFO aims to "carry that momentum into fiscal 2027", his comment on strengthening demand is quoted under Leadership, and the fourth-quarter outlook gives fiscal 2027 a starting point above the third quarter. Against it, FY27E consensus revenue of $18.2B is more than four quarters at the fourth-quarter outlook of $4.3 billion would bring, so consensus needs sequential growth to continue through fiscal 2027, which would make it a third straight year of expansion. That fiscal 2026 consensus already matches the company's outlook supports the Street's numbers without settling fiscal 2027.

The Bull case carries 20%. It needs the condition in its driver, investors looking through fiscal 2027 to further growth, and nothing in the outlook reaches that far.

The Bear case carries 25%, argued on the Bear itself. In the table, FY22's +64.2% was followed by a stall in FY23 (+2.4%) and then the FY24 decline set out under Risks. ADI is now in its second year of growth with margins at the cyclical high described under Financials, the point where a stall would cost most. Against that, the outlook points higher and the current data show no turn, so we hold the Bear at one in four rather than higher.

The weighted result is expected upside of -0.8% against a Bear-case downside of -46.9%, which derives HOLD. The call is close, and nearer to SELL than to BUY. The deciding split is Base against Bear: moving ten points of weight from Base to Bear would derive SELL. For more Bear weight, margins sit at a cyclical high, the shares have run hard and distributors carry more than half of revenue. For less, the outlook points up and nothing yet shows demand turning. We judge the current evidence too positive to put a turn above one in four, so the label is HOLD. With a Bear this deep, BUY is out of reach at the current price.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: ADI reports one segment, and its 10-Q splits revenue by end market and by channel. In the fiscal third quarter 2026, Industrial was 49% of revenue (45% a year earlier), Automotive 25% (30%), Communications 16% (12%) and Consumer 10% (13%), so the mix is shifting toward the two end markets that grew faster than the company total. Distributors, which buy products with the intention of reselling them, carried 58% of revenue against 55%, and direct customers, mainly original equipment manufacturers, 39% against 43%. ADI says the distributor share rose "primarily due to the increase in the percentage of revenue from our Industrial end market." The 2026 proxy statement puts "Business-to-Business Revenue" at ~87% for fiscal 2025, so demand rests largely on business spending. The shift makes ADI more geared to industrial demand and data center spending than a year ago, adding growth in an upswing and exposure in a downturn, and leaves more than half of revenue reflecting distributor purchases rather than direct end demand (see Risks).

moatFactors.name: Cash margins through the cycle
moatFactors.body: Across FY21–FY25, free-cash-flow margin never fell below 28.9%, and it was 33.1% in the FY24 downturn. Part of that resilience came from spending less, not from pricing: capital expenditure fell to $0.7B in FY24 from $1.3B in FY23, and the margin's low point came in FY23, the year of the larger outlay. Gross margin, the line that shows pricing, fell to 57.1% in FY24 from 64.0%. What survives is a gross margin that held at that level in a year revenue fell 23.4%, which we read as real but not exceptional pricing power.

moatFactors.name: Breadth and R&D commitment
moatFactors.body: ADI sells many product families into several end markets through several channels, so no single application carries the business. The 2026 proxy says ADI "invested a record amount to research and development in fiscal year 2025" to "further extend the technical and market leadership of our core analog, mixed signal, and power portfolio." Breadth backed by sustained R&D is the base of the franchise. The limit is that this evidence is the company's own description, and without peer data we cannot show the portfolio out-earns rivals.

moatFactors.name: Manufacturing footprint
moatFactors.body: The CEO cites "manufacturing agility" as part of ADI's advantage, and the release refers to "our hybrid manufacturing model". The gross-margin gain described under Financials came "primarily" from higher utilization of ADI's own fixed manufacturing costs, together with favorable mix. Those fixed costs let margins rise with demand and weigh on them when demand falls. The fiscal 2025 10-K lists significant operations and manufacturing outside the United States, including in Ireland, the Philippines, Thailand and Malaysia, which adds trade and geopolitical exposure.

moatFactors.name: Return on the capital base
moatFactors.body: Fiscal 2025 net income of $2.3B came on total equity of $33.8B, a modest return on the book the company carries even in a recovery year. Measured on free cash flow the return looks better, but the modest return on book equity is why we stop short of WIDE: the evidence shows a franchise with solid margins, not one earning exceptional returns on the capital invested in it.

businessMoat.durability:
We rate the moat NARROW, for the reasons set out in the factors above. The main threat to its durability is China. The fiscal 2025 10-K says export restrictions may cause customers to "replace our products with products from another supplier that is not subject to the export restrictions or focus on building indigenous semiconductor capacity to reduce reliance on U.S. suppliers."

The 10-Q also lists "our ability to compete successfully in the markets in which we operate" among the factors that could change results. Over a five-year view we expect the franchise to keep its margins in most markets, with the business tied to China the part most exposed to erosion.

points: Industrial, close to half of revenue, grew {+ 53% +} year over year in the fiscal third quarter 2026. The company says all Industrial sub-markets grew, "with test equipment and aerospace and defense representing the highest growth." Growth that broad in an end market of that size is the core of the upswing. The counter-case is concentration: Industrial's share of revenue rose over the year, as the business section shows, so more of the upswing now rides on one end market (see Risks for the channel exposure).

Communications grew {+ 84% +} year over year in the quarter and 72% over the nine months, ahead of the other three end markets. The company says "the strongest growth within Communications came from the data center sub-market, driven by artificial intelligence-related infrastructure investments." In our view this driver has a better chance than the others of outlasting the cycle, but the company ties it to one theme of customer investment, and Communications is still smaller than Industrial or Automotive. A pause in that investment would hit it directly.

Automotive grew 16% and Consumer 6% in the quarter, both slower than the company as a whole. Automotive's quarterly rate beat its 9% nine-month rate, so it picked up in the third quarter, while Consumer's lagged its 18% nine-month rate, so it slowed. Consumer is the one end market where momentum is fading.

On August 19, 2026, ADI guided fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue to $4.3 billion, plus or minus $100 million, above the third quarter even at the low end. It expects reported operating margin of approximately 42.6%, plus or minus 150 bps, and reported EPS of $3.14, plus or minus $0.15 (adjusted: approximately 52.0% and $3.86). The CFO called it a "record fourth quarter outlook", while the company notes actual results "may differ materially." The outlook supports the near term, not fiscal 2027.

Consensus expects FY26E revenue of $15.1B (+37%), in line with nine-month revenue plus the fourth-quarter outlook midpoint, and FY27E revenue of $18.2B with EPS of $16.35. Fiscal 2026 is largely set by the outlook; fiscal 2027 is where the debate sits, and the valuation section weighs the evidence for it.

management.leadership:
According to the 2026 proxy statement, Vincent Roche is Chief Executive Officer and Chair of the Board of Directors, and Richard C. Puccio, Jr. is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. The other named executive officers for fiscal 2025 were Martin Cotter (Senior Vice President, Vertical Business Units), Vivek Jain (Executive Vice President, Global Operations and Technology) and Katsu Nakamura (Senior Vice President and Chief Customer Officer).

In the August 19, 2026 release, Roche said ADI delivered results "exceeding the midpoint of our revenue, margin, and earnings outlook," and Puccio said "Demand continued to strengthen across our product portfolio and regions throughout the third quarter." We take the beat on the company's word. Roche's description of "a unique advantage to create, deliver, and capture value in the AI era" is forward-looking, and we do not score it.

The team is executing well in an upswing. The proxy excerpt gives no tenures, so we cannot say who set policy in the last downturn; the company's FY24 results, covered under capital allocation, show how ADI responded then.
management.capitalAllocation:
ADI returns most of its cash to shareholders. In fiscal 2025 it repurchased $2.2B of stock and paid $1.9B in dividends; the 2026 proxy reports more than $4 billion returned that year, more than $24B over ten years and a 10-year dividend CAGR of 9.5%. In the fiscal third quarter 2026 it returned $1.7 billion, and on August 19, 2026 the board declared a $1.10 quarterly dividend, which was payable on September 15, 2026.

The pace now runs ahead of cash generation. The release's trailing-twelve-month cash-return table shows dividends and repurchases together exceeding free cash flow of $4.9 billion, while cash and short-term investments have fallen since fiscal year-end, as the balance-sheet discussion shows. The acquisition discussed under Risks adds a cost the documents do not yet quantify.

FY24 shows how the company flexes. Repurchases fell to $0.6B from $3.0B in FY23, while dividends rose to $1.8B from $1.7B. Protecting the dividend and flexing the buyback is the right order for shareholders, and we expect it to repeat if the cycle turns, which makes buybacks, not the dividend, the lever at risk.
management.governance:
Governance evidence comes from the 2026 proxy statement, which covers fiscal 2025 pay and reports ownership as of January 8, 2026. Vincent Roche holds both the CEO and Chair roles. The excerpt does not show board independence or any lead director arrangement, so we cannot judge the counterweight to a combined CEO and Chair; on its face, the combination concentrates authority.

Target pay comprises base salary, a variable cash incentive, time-based RSUs, relative TSR PRSUs and financial metric PRSUs. The proxy describes "a significant portion of the total target compensation" for executive officers as "variable, performance-based incentive compensation"; the excerpt cuts off before the mix figures, so that lean toward performance is the company's own account. Base salary and time-based RSUs are the parts not tied to performance. The relative TSR PRSUs tie part of pay to shareholder returns, which is the right alignment for shareholders.

The proxy reports no related person transactions requiring disclosure under Item 404 since the beginning of fiscal year 2025 through the proxy date, and a written policy under which the Audit Committee reviews related person transactions above $120,000. For outside holders the picture is clean on related parties and, by the company's account, performance-weighted on pay, with the combined CEO and Chair role as the one structural point against.
management.insiderOwnership:
No holder comes close to control. As of January 8, 2026, the proxy lists two holders of 5% or more: Vanguard Group Inc. with 49,618,676 shares beneficially owned, or 10.2%, and BlackRock Inc. with 38,733,607 shares, or 7.9%. Both rest on Schedule 13G amendments that report ownership as of February 28, 2025 for Vanguard and December 31, 2023 for BlackRock, so both figures are dated.

Insider stakes are small. All directors and executive officers as a group (15 persons) beneficially owned 1,771,101 shares, less than 1% of the stock, and no individual comes close to that level; Ray Stata's 791,897 shares top the individual lines in the table. Vincent Roche's total beneficial ownership of 790,854 shares includes 686,226 shares acquirable within 60 days, so most of his position takes that form.

For outside holders, ADI is widely held, and insiders' alignment comes mainly through pay design rather than large personal stakes. That puts more weight on the board's oversight of capital allocation.

idiosyncratic: Operating leverage in reverse. The fixed-cost utilization that the company names as the primary driver of this year's gross-margin gain works the other way when demand falls. FY24 shows the scale: revenue fell 23.4%, operating margin dropped to 21.6%, and diluted EPS fell to $3.28 from $6.55. With trailing margins now above FY23's, a downturn from here would start from a higher base and could cut earnings just as sharply. This is the main risk to the stock, and the Bear case prices it.

China and export restrictions. The fiscal 2025 10-K says export restrictions "have impacted our revenues and results of operations in China and elsewhere" and that ADI expects they "may continue to have direct and indirect adverse impacts." Without a China revenue figure we cannot size the exposure. It is an ongoing drag with a risk of escalation.

Distributor buying. With distributors carrying more than half of revenue, as described in the business section, reported revenue depends partly on distributor purchasing decisions. The 10-Q lists "performance of independent distributors" and the risk that "products may be diverted from our authorized distribution channels" among factors that could change results, and the 10-K names customers that "amass large inventories of our products" as one response to export restrictions. We cannot see channel inventory, so a correction would arrive with little notice.

Acquisition integration. ADI recorded transaction costs in the third quarter for the acquisition of Empower Semiconductor, Inc., and its price and timing are not stated in the documents we draw on. The 10-Q lists "unanticipated difficulties or expenditures relating to integrating acquired businesses" among the factors that could cause results to differ. Alongside the cash trends covered under capital allocation, a large deal would narrow the cushion further; we rate the risk moderate until terms are known.
risks.systemic:
ADI's results follow the broad semiconductor and industrial cycle. The 10-Q lists "changes in demand for semiconductor products" and "economic, political, legal and regulatory uncertainty or conflicts" among the factors that could change results, and the fiscal 2025 10-K adds inflation, tariffs and trade restrictions, high interest rates and "slower economic growth or recession."

Trade policy bears directly on ADI. The 10-K notes that in April 2025 the Department of Commerce launched a Section 232 investigation into imported semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and that the global trade situation "continues to be highly dynamic." With significant manufacturing outside the United States, as the moat section notes, any measures that follow could raise ADI's costs or weigh on its sales. The 10-K also cites tensions across the Taiwan Strait that "may adversely affect our operations in Taiwan, our customers and the technology industry supply chain."

The data center exposure discussed under Growth adds an industry-wide investment theme to this list. These risks are shared across the sector; ADI's breadth spreads them but does not remove them.

body: We rate Analog Devices HOLD with a target range of $400–$470. For a current holder, that means keeping the position: the upswing is still running and the weighted value sits within the range. For a new buyer, it means waiting for better evidence on fiscal 2027 or a lower price. The operating leverage that has lifted margins is the business's own cyclical risk, and at this price the shares leave little room for it.

We would move to BUY if the shares fell to well below the lowest Street target of $365.00 with FY27E consensus intact, or on a smaller pullback if the fourth-quarter results and the next outlook made a fiscal 2027 stall look unlikely. We would move to SELL if fourth-quarter revenue fell below the bottom of the outlook range or the next outlook pointed below the FY27E consensus path, or if the shares rose above our target range without higher estimates.
